opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, partly because I've spent time on architecture work myself, with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, and I know how messy the real process is. So let me say what would convince *me*.

First, the bar shouldn't be "it beat a benchmark by half a percent." That's hyperparameter search with extra steps, and we've had neural architecture search for years. Searching a predefined space of building blocks isn't proposing a new architecture. It's recombining old ones.

What would convince me has a few layers.

**One: the idea has to come with a reason.** When people proposed the Transformer, or residual connections, or even KANs, there was a story. Residual connections came from thinking about optimization and identity mappings. KANs came from taking the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem seriously and asking what happens if you put learnable activations on edges instead of nodes. So I'd want the AI system to give me an inductive bias it believes is missing, explain why that bias should matter for some class of problems, and only then show me the architecture. If it can articulate the "why" before the "what," that's much closer to how real research works.

**Two: it should predict where it fails.** A good scientist knows the limits of their own idea. If the system says "this will help on tasks with compositional structure but will hurt on noisy, high-entropy data, and here's the experiment to check," and that prediction holds up, that's very convincing. Anyone can claim wins. Correctly predicting your own losses shows understanding.

**Three: it should transfer and get adopted.** The real test of an architecture is whether other people pick it up and it survives contact with problems the inventor never imagined. So in the long run, the convincing demonstration is sociological as much as technical. Do human researchers, or other AI agents, find it useful enough to build on, in domains outside the original paper?

**Four, and this is my physics bias: does it reveal something?** The architectures I find most beautiful aren't just effective. They tell you something about the structure of the problem. If an AI system proposed an architecture, and when we looked inside the trained model we found it had discovered a symmetry, a conservation law, or a modular decomposition we didn't know about, I'd be genuinely excited. Then it isn't just engineering, it's science.

I should be honest that we aren't fully there yet. Current systems are getting good at the inner loop: implementing ideas, running experiments, debugging, sweeping. The outer loop, deciding which question is worth asking and which inductive bias is missing, is still largely human taste. So the moment an AI system shows real *taste*, picking a direction most experts would have dismissed and turning out to be right, that's the demonstration I'd find most convincing. It's also the hardest one to fake.

r001.rationale: The response says an architecture needs a reasoned case for its inductive bias and explains that adoption depends on others finding it useful and building on it.

r002.rationale: It rejects a small benchmark gain as insufficient, but does not propose an approximately ten-percentage-point improvement over a domain leaderboard best.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because "AI proposes a new architecture" is one of those claims that's very easy to make and very hard to make honestly.

Let me start with what would not convince me. If you give a system a search space like "pick the number of layers, pick the width, pick the activation function, pick the attention pattern," and it finds a combination that gets 0.3% better on some benchmark, that is not a new architecture. That is hyperparameter tuning with extra steps. Neural architecture search has been doing this for years. It's useful, but nobody would say NAS "invented" anything, because the space of possible answers was fully specified by the human beforehand. The creativity was in writing the search space.

So the first thing I'd look for is: did the system step outside the space the human gave it? Did it introduce a new primitive, a new kind of operation, a new way of composing things, that wasn't on the menu? When I think about the architectures that actually mattered historically, like convolutions, attention, residual connections, normalization, each of them was conceptually a new object, not a new setting of an old dial. If an AI system only ever recombines existing blocks, I'd say it's doing engineering, not science.

The second thing is explanation. A real architecture comes with a reason. Transformers didn't just work; there's a story about why attention lets you route information across positions, why residuals help gradient flow, and so on. If a system hands me a block diagram and a loss curve and says "trust me," I'm actually less convinced than if it hands me a worse architecture plus a correct mechanistic argument for why it should behave a certain way. Because the mechanism is what generalizes. Benchmark numbers on one dataset don't tell me whether the idea will survive at a different scale or on a different modality. So I'd want the system to make a prediction: "this should help in regime X and hurt in regime Y," and then I'd test that prediction. If it holds, that's a sign there's genuine understanding, not pattern matching.

Third, and this is where I'd be strictest, is contamination and scale. If the "new" architecture is something that exists in a 2023 arXiv paper the model was trained on, that doesn't count, obviously, and this is surprisingly hard to rule out. And if it only works at toy scale, I'd be cautious too, because a lot of ideas look great on CIFAR and then evaporate. The honest demonstration would be: a novel idea, with a mechanism, that holds up when a skeptical human lab with real compute tries to replicate it and scale it.

And actually, I'd add one more thing, which is a bit more personal. I'd want to see the system reject ideas. Most of what a good researcher does is kill their own bad ideas quickly. A system that proposes a hundred architectures and says "here, go test them" has offloaded the hard part onto humans. A system that proposes five, explains why it discarded the other ninety-five, and is right about most of those discards, is doing something closer to research. The taste is in the no, not the yes.

So the convincing demo, for me, isn't a single number. It's a new primitive, a mechanistic story, a falsifiable prediction that survives, and evidence that the system has judgment about what not to try. If I saw all four at once, I'd genuinely update. I haven't seen all four yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a mechanistic explanation can make even a worse-performing architecture more convincing than benchmark results alone, and that the explanation should support predictions that hold up. This communicates the need for a reasoned case when performance is not decisive.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not propose a roughly ten-percentage-point improvement over a previous leaderboard best; it instead says even a 0.3% benchmark gain would not establish a new architecture.

astra-6.text:
I think a convincing demonstration would be that it proposes an architecture we didn’t already have in mind, and then shows why that architecture is useful. Just generating something different is a pretty low bar—you can randomly change connections and get a new architecture. The hard part is finding a change that matters.

So I would give it a problem with a clear limitation in existing architectures, let it propose and test ideas, and then evaluate the result on tasks it didn’t use during that search. You’d want strong baselines, comparable compute budgets, and ablations showing that the proposed architectural change actually causes the improvement.

What would excite me most is if it also gives us an insight: ‘This assumption is unnecessary,’ or ‘This structure is better suited to this kind of problem.’ Then we can test that explanation independently. It doesn’t have to beat every existing model. A new architecture that works reliably in a meaningful setting, and teaches us something about why, would already be quite convincing.

r001.rationale: The response says a new architecture need not beat every existing model, but should show why it is useful and offer an independently testable insight. That is a reasoned case for adoption without requiring an overwhelming performance advantage.

r002.rationale: The response gives no specific domain or roughly ten-percentage-point leaderboard improvement threshold; it explicitly says the architecture need not beat every existing model.

sol-6.1.text:
I would want it to discover an architecture that we didn’t already tell it to look for, and then demonstrate that it works. That means implementing it, training it, and comparing it against strong baselines under the same compute budget. A plausible-looking diagram or an interesting name wouldn’t be enough.

The really convincing part would be if it could explain what limitation the architecture addresses, make predictions about when it should help, and then verify those predictions through experiments and ablations. Ideally, the improvement would carry over to tasks that weren’t used during the search. Then we would have evidence that the system found a useful architectural principle, rather than just a configuration that happened to win one benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response calls for explaining the architecture’s purpose and validating its predictions, but does not state that an architecture without an overwhelming performance advantage needs this reasoned case to persuade people to adopt it.

r002.rationale: The response mentions comparing against strong baselines but gives no roughly ten-percentage-point improvement target or specific domain leaderboard.
